title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals used generative AI to impersonate an immigration attorney in South Florida by cloning his voice and identity, then used those deepfakes to target immigrants on social media with fraudulent legal services. This is a case of AI-enabled impersonation deployed in the wild without authentication or verification that the person offering services was who they claimed to be. The scam worked because social media platforms did not require proof of professional credentials before allowing someone to solicit legal services.

Voice cloning and deepfake technology made the impersonation convincing enough that victims sent money for services that were never provided. Scammers sourced personal information from social media to tailor pitches to their targets. A human verification step, such as requiring professional licenses to be confirmed before offering legal services, or calling the real attorney's verified office number to confirm engagement, would have stopped these scams before money changed hands.

It is not established whether the social media platforms where these scams operated had policies against impersonation or how they enforced them, nor is it established what specific security or identity verification measures might have been technically feasible at the point of service solicitation.

summary:
# Summary

Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence and deepfake technology to commit scams across Georgia and South Florida. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report found that Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to target immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scheme. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints totaling more than $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers use generative AI to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research personal relationships to make scams more convincing. Common schemes include grandparent scams using voice cloning, romance scams, and fake emergency calls. To protect themselves, consumers should establish code words with family members, verify urgent requests by contacting people directly through known numbers, never send money based solely on phone calls, monitor accounts closely, and report suspected scams to law enforcement and the FBI.
